claims.text: Higher weekly physical activity measured in MET-hours is associated with a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus in men.
Increased weekly time spent watching television is significantly associated with higher risk for type 2 diabetes mellitus in men.
The positive association between television watching time and type 2 diabetes risk persists after adjustment for body mass index.

evidence.description: Adjusted relative risks for type 2 diabetes across increasing quintiles of MET-hours per week were 1.00, 0.78, 0.65, 0.58, and 0.51 (P for trend < .001).
Adjusted relative risks of diabetes across categories of average hours spent watching TV per week (0-1, 2-10, 11-20, 21-40, and >40) were 1.00, 1.66, 1.64, 2.16, and 2.87 (P for trend < .001).
After adjustment for body mass index, the relative risk comparing extreme TV watching categories was 2.31 (P for trend = .01).

methodologies.name: Prospective cohort study using self-reported questionnaires
methodologies.description: A 10-year prospective follow-up study tracking 37,918 men using physical activity questionnaires and biennial TV watching questionnaires.
datasets: 37,918 male health professionals cohort (347,040 person-years of follow-up)
conditions: Free of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer at baseline
